title: Decorator and Proxy
goal: By the end you can stack decorators and predict what their order does, use Kotlin `by` without falling into its forwarding trap, write a dynamic proxy that unwraps exceptions, and explain why a proxy never sees the calls an object makes on itself.
opening:
A customer at the corner shop buys a teapot as a present. The shopkeeper puts it in its box, wraps the box in gift paper and ties a ribbon around it. Then Pedal Post's rider weighs it, scans the label and rides off, quite unmoved by the bow. A wrapped parcel is still a parcel. The teapot didn't change, and the courier handles it exactly as before.

In the back office, the shop's manager is too busy to answer the phone, so a receptionist answers for her. Callers dial the same number as always. The receptionist checks who's calling, takes messages and puts the right calls through.

Code wraps objects in both ways. The easy trap is to think a wrapper is invisible. It isn't: the order of the layers can change a price, and some calls never pass the receptionist at all.

The last lesson ended on a wrapper that keeps the interface exactly as it is. In this lesson, we'll build two: a decorator, which adds one thing and passes the call on, and a proxy, which stands in front of an object and decides how to call it. Kotlin's `by` will write the passing-on for us. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: A proxy times every call made to the shop's `Stockroom`. Through the proxy, you call `pickBoth("tea", "jam")`. Inside the real stockroom, `pickBoth` calls its own `pick` method twice. How many calls does the proxy time?
options: None: a proxy only times calls that return a value
warmup.why: The proxy is a separate object, and it only handles calls made on it. The shop's code calls `pickBoth` on the proxy, so that call is timed. Inside, `pick(first)` means `this.pick(first)`, and `this` is the real stockroom, so both inner calls go straight past the proxy. The last section of this lesson shows the two paths, and the Try it in the third section prints the trace `[pickBoth]`.

sections.h: Kotlin's by writes the forwarding, and never calls you back
sections.body:
A delivery fee has one method, so a lambda can decorate it. Most interfaces have more. A hand-written decorator for `Map` in Java must pass on every method (`get`, `put`, `remove`, `size`, `entrySet` and a dozen more) just to change one. That passing-on is called **forwarding**, and it's most of the code.

Kotlin's **class delegation** writes the forwarding for you. Say we want a map that counts how often something is put into it:

```kotlin
class CountingMap<K, V>(private val inner: MutableMap<K, V> = HashMap()) : MutableMap<K, V> by inner {
    var puts = 0
    override fun put(key: K, value: V): V? { puts++; return inner.put(key, value) }
}
```

```java
// Java has no `by`. The short way is inheritance, and HashMap's insides decide what you count.
class CountingMap<K, V> extends HashMap<K, V> {
    int puts;
    @Override public V put(K key, V value) { puts++; return super.put(key, value); }
}
```

Read `: MutableMap<K, V> by inner` as "for every method of `MutableMap` I don't write myself, call the same method on `inner`". The object `by` forwards to is called the **delegate**. The Kotlin docs call delegation "a good alternative to implementation inheritance", where inheritance means taking a parent class's code with `extends`.

Now predict. We call `put("tea", 1)` and then `putAll` with two more entries. What is `puts`? The `CountingMapDemo` in the Try it prints:

```text
CountingMap: puts=1, size=3
```

One, while the map holds three. The compiler forwarded `putAll` to `inner.putAll`, and `inner` is a plain `HashMap` that has never heard of our `put`. The docs say so: overridden members "do not get called from the members of the delegate object". The delegate never calls you back. To count every insertion, override `putAll` too, and `putIfAbsent`, `compute` and `merge`.

That surprise is also the benefit. With inheritance, the count depends on how the parent class is written today. `HashMap.putAll` happens not to call `put`, so the Java version also prints 1. But `HashSet.addAll` does call `add`, so a set that counts in both methods counts each item twice, and the Java twin prints `added=6` for three items. *Effective Java*, the well-known book of Java advice, builds its item 18, "Favor composition over inheritance", on that very bug. With `by`, the delegate never calls back into your code, so a JDK update can't change your numbers.

**The delegate never calls your overrides. Override every method that should behave differently.**

The JDK has a read-only decorator you meet often: `Collections.unmodifiableList`. It forwards reads and throws on writes. It's a **view**, which means it reads through to the list it wraps, so later changes to that list show up in it. For a frozen copy, use `List.copyOf`. Kotlin's `List` is weaker still: a read-only type on the same object, with no wrapper at all:

```java
List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(shopping);
shopping.add("jam");           // the view shows it too
view.add("tea");               // UnsupportedOperationException
```

```kotlin
val view: List<String> = shopping          // the same object, with a read-only type
shopping += "jam"                           // the view shows it too
(view as MutableList).add("tea")            // works: nothing guards it
```

A decorator works when we know the interface and want one extra behavior. Sometimes we want the same extra behavior, such as timing, on every method of every interface, without writing a class for each one.

aside.title: Why does a framework annotation sometimes do nothing?
aside.body: If you write web services, your framework probably hands out proxies like ours. In Spring, a popular Java framework, an annotation such as `@Transactional` (run this method inside a database transaction, a group of changes that all succeed or all fail together) is carried out by a proxy that stands in front of your class. So a call from one of its methods to another, through `this`, skips the proxy, exactly like `pickBoth` calling `pick`; the Spring docs say self-invocation "will bypass the advice". Their preferred fix is to move the inner method to another class, so the call crosses a proxy. Quarkus, another framework, does intercept such calls, as a feature its docs mark non-standard, so the same code can behave differently in the two. And because Kotlin classes are final unless marked `open`, Kotlin Spring projects add the `kotlin-spring` compiler plugin, which opens Spring-annotated classes so the framework's subclass proxies can override them.

compare.title: A timing decorator for a three-method courier desk

java.title: TimedCourierDesk.java

kotlin.title: TimedCourierDesk.kt

compare.note: The behavior is the same: time `book`, pass `track` and `cancel` straight on. What differs is who writes the passing-on. Java makes you type `track` and `cancel`, and Kotlin's `by inner` generates them. That matters again when the interface grows. Add `void reschedule(String ref)` to `CourierDesk` and the Java decorator stops compiling until someone decides what it should do with the new method. The Kotlin one forwards it without a word, untimed. Neither is wrong, but know which one you have. And remember that `by` never calls you back: if the real desk's `track` calls its own `book`, that inner booking isn't timed. Kotlin makes the hand-written forwarding class unnecessary; it doesn't make Decorator unnecessary.

worked.title: Make a retry proxy safe for orders

steps.say: A teammate wrapped the shop's order line in the retrying proxy from this lesson, with three attempts. The warehouse sometimes takes 2 seconds to answer, and the shop's code gives up after 1.5 seconds. Before reading on, say what the customer gets on a slow afternoon.

Attempt one gave up on our side, but the warehouse took the order anyway. Attempts two and three are new orders, so the customer gets two or three loaves. A retry is safe only for a call you can repeat without changing the result: the usual word for that is idempotent. Make that visible in the interface by marking the methods that are safe to repeat.

The handler reads the mark before its loop, and unmarked methods get exactly one attempt. Why does `method.isAnnotationPresent` work here, even though the mark sits on the interface and not on `WarehouseOrderLine`? Because the `Method` the proxy receives is the interface's method.

Now make placing an order safe to repeat. The caller picks an order number once and sends it with every attempt. The warehouse keeps its first answer for each number and hands it back for a repeat, instead of taking a second order. The number must come from the caller: one made up inside the retry loop would be new on each attempt and protect nothing.

lab.title: A delivery fee decorator chain and a timing proxy
steps: Run the tests once. All twelve fail with `UnsupportedOperationException`.
In `DeliveryFee`, write `perKm` as a lambda: `d -> d.km() * centsPerKm`. Then write each default method so it returns a new lambda that calls `cents(d)` (the fee being decorated) and adds one rule.

In `TimingProxy.wrap`, build an `InvocationHandler` and pass it to `Proxy.newProxyInstance`. Forward methods declared by `Object` without timing them. For the rest, read the clock, call `method.invoke(target, args)`, read the clock again and report `Interface.method`.
Catch `InvocationTargetException`, report the call as failed, and rethrow `e.getCause()`.
Run the tests until all twelve pass. Then read the self-invocation test and explain to yourself why only `bookTwice` is reported.
hints: Inside a default method, a bare `cents(d)` means `this.cents(d)`, where `this` is the fee you are decorating. The lambda you return captures it.
"Over 5 kg" means strictly more: a parcel of exactly 5,000 g pays no surcharge, and a test checks it.

`method.getDeclaringClass() == Object.class` is true for `toString`, `equals` and `hashCode` on a JDK proxy. Report with `iface.getSimpleName() + "." + method.getName()`. `throw e.getCause();` compiles because `InvocationHandler.invoke` is declared `throws Throwable`.

drill.prompt: Close this page. Write `static <T> T logging(Class<T> iface, T target, List<String> log)` (in Kotlin, `inline fun <reified T : Any> logging(target: T, log: MutableList<String>): T`). It returns a JDK dynamic proxy that adds each method name to `log`, forwards the call, and lets the target's own exception reach the caller unwrapped. Then compare. Did you remember the unwrap?

alt.title: Kotlin

recap: A decorator has the same interface as the object it wraps, adds one behavior and passes the call on. `java.io` streams and `Collections.unmodifiableList` are decorators.
The order of the layers changes results: capping before the heavy-parcel surcharge turns an 8.00 delivery into 11.00, and retrying outside logging logs every attempt.
Kotlin `by` generates the forwarding methods, but the delegate never calls your overrides: `putAll` skips your `put`.
A dynamic proxy (`java.lang.reflect.Proxy`) sends every call on an interface to one handler. Unwrap `InvocationTargetException`, or callers get `UndeclaredThrowableException`.

The limit: a proxy sees only the calls made on it, so an object's calls on `this` skip it, and it knows only a method's name and arguments. It can't tell a status check from an order that must happen once unless you mark the method.
closing:
We started at the counter, with a teapot in gift paper and a receptionist in the back office. In code, the paper became decorators around a delivery fee, where moving one layer changed the price, and Kotlin's `by` wrote the passing-on for us. The receptionist became a proxy that answers for every method, and misses every call an object makes on itself.

Now look in your own code for a class that implements an interface and passes most calls to a field of the same type. That's a decorator. Check what order it's stacked in, and whether a test pins that order.

Next, we'll stop wrapping one object and start building trees of them. How can a box full of smaller boxes answer "what do you cost?" as if it were one parcel?

quiz.q: `DeliveryFee.perKm(50).plusFixed(200).cappedAt(800).heavySurcharge(5_000, 300)` prices a 12 kg parcel going 20 km. What does it return, in cents?
quiz.why: Work from the inside out: 20 km at 50 is 1,000, plus 200 to start is 1,200, capped at 800, and then the surcharge adds 300 after the cap. Total 1,100. The tempting 800 is what you get with the cap as the outermost layer.

quiz.q: `class LoggedOrderBook(private val inner: OrderBook) : OrderBook by inner` overrides only `write(order)` to log a line. The real order book's `writeAll(orders)` calls its own `write` for each order. You call `logged.writeAll(listOf(a, b, c))`. How many lines are logged?
quiz.why: `writeAll` is forwarded to `inner.writeAll`, and `inner` calls its own `write`, never the override in `LoggedOrderBook`. The delegate never calls you back. To log bulk writes, override `writeAll` too.

quiz.q: An `InvocationHandler` does `return method.invoke(target, args);` with no try/catch. The target throws `IllegalArgumentException`. What does the caller of the proxy catch?
quiz.why: `method.invoke` wraps the target's exception in `InvocationTargetException`, a checked exception. The interface method doesn't declare it, so the proxy wraps it again in `UndeclaredThrowableException`. Catch the `InvocationTargetException` in the handler and rethrow `getCause()`.

quiz.q: You need to record how long every method takes on six different interfaces (about forty methods in all), with one rule for all of them. Which tool fits best?
options: A dynamic proxy, or your framework's interceptor
A hand-written decorator class per interface
Kotlin `by` with one override per method
quiz.why: One rule applied to every method of many interfaces is what a proxy is for: one handler, written once. Hand-written decorators and `by` overrides mean forty copies of the same timing code, and an adapter changes the interface, which you don't want here.

quiz.q: From *Adapter and Facade*: which of these wrappers is an adapter rather than a decorator?
quiz.why: An adapter gives the wrapped object a different interface: the shop's `Warehouse` port instead of the old program's item numbers and two-digit codes. The other three keep the interface of the object they wrap and add or restrict behavior, which is what a decorator does.

flashcards.front: What makes a wrapper a decorator?
flashcards.back: It has the same interface as the object it wraps, adds one behavior, and passes the call on. Callers can't tell it's there.

flashcards.front: Retry decorator outside a logging decorator, and the line is busy twice before it books: how many log lines?
flashcards.back: Three. The inner decorator sees every attempt; the outer one sees one booking.

flashcards.front: `CountingMap : MutableMap by inner` overrides `put`. After `put` once and `putAll` of two entries, what is `puts`?
flashcards.back: 1. `putAll` is forwarded to `inner`, which never calls your override.
A read-through view: writes throw, but later changes to `list` show up. Use `List.copyOf` for a frozen copy.
`method.invoke` wraps the target's exception. If the wrapper escapes, callers get `UndeclaredThrowableException` instead of the real error.

flashcards.front: A proxied object calls its own method through `this`. Does the proxy handle that call?
flashcards.back: No. Self-invocation goes straight to the real object; a proxy only sees calls made on it.

flashcards.front: Decorator and Proxy have the same shape. What tells them apart?
flashcards.back: Intent. A decorator adds behavior the caller wants; a proxy controls whether, when and how the real object is called.

terms.plain: A wrapper with the same interface as the object inside it, adding one behavior.
A stand-in with the same interface that controls whether and how the real object is called: retrying, timing, checking.
A class made while the program runs by `java.lang.reflect.Proxy`, which implements interfaces and routes every call to one handler.
The one method, `invoke(proxy, method, args)`, that a dynamic proxy calls for every interface method.
Kotlin syntax that generates the forwarding methods of an interface, sending each call to a delegate object.
An object calling its own method through `this`, which skips any proxy in front of it.
A wrapper that reads through to the collection it wraps, so later changes to that collection show up in it.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate wraps the stockroom in a timing proxy and says: "`pickBoth` shows up in the timings, but the two `pick` calls inside it never do. The proxy is broken." Explain what is happening, and give two ways to get the inner calls timed.
explain_back.answer: The proxy isn't broken. It's a separate object that stands in front of the real stockroom, and it can only handle calls made on it. The shop's code calls `pickBoth` on the proxy, so that call is timed and forwarded. Inside the real stockroom, `pick(first)` is `this.pick(first)`, and `this` is the real object, so the two inner calls never pass the proxy. To time them, either make them through the proxy, so the caller calls `pick` twice itself, or move `pick` to its own object behind its own proxy and let `pickBoth` call that object. Frameworks that put proxies in front of our classes behave the same way, which is why an annotation on a method called through `this` can silently do nothing.

deeper.body:
JDK proxy classes are final, extend `java.lang.reflect.Proxy`, and can be detected with `Proxy.isProxyClass`. Their names aren't specified, but names starting with `$Proxy` are reserved for them, which is why stack traces show `$Proxy0.book`, as the demo's did. A proxy also sends `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` to the handler, so a proxy and its target are different objects to a `HashSet` unless the handler forwards those methods. The lab's timing proxy forwards them on purpose.

Resilience4j, a widely used Java library for calls that may fail, is a decorator library by design. Its README says it provides "higher-order functions (decorators)" for any functional interface, lambda or method reference, and that you can stack more than one. You wrap a `Supplier` in a retry, wrap the result in a circuit breaker (a switch that stops calling a service that keeps failing), and so on. The order question from this lesson comes back: a retry outside the breaker retries calls the breaker refused, and a retry inside it counts every attempt as a call. Lesson 11 of this track, *Concurrency patterns that tie it all together*, builds a breaker by hand.

The GoF book lists several kinds of proxy by job. A virtual proxy creates the expensive real object only on the first call, like the lazy price list in lesson 1 of this track. A remote proxy makes an object in another program look local. A protection proxy checks who is calling. All three have the same structure as a decorator, which is why intent, not shape, is how people tell them apart.
